_comment: DEMO, not the default: one access point per hall, and every command arrives through it.
One option turns this on: `wifi.enabled`. It is false in `mecanum_lab/types.py`, because
the graded runs of both experiments are calibrated on a link that delivers everything at
once, and off means nothing happens at all -- no radio is built, no random number is drawn,
no `/link` is published. This file is the demo that switches it on:
./lab sim --world production --config config/demo_wifi.json
# drive it, look at layer n
./lab run --world production --config config/demo_wifi.json --robot muster \
--controller student/link_autonomy_example.py --seconds 60
# drive it on its own, 60 s of it
In the window the layer `n` draws the access point as a box with two arcs, one line from it
to every robot and a bar over each robot: q, the dBm behind it, how many walls the line
crosses, the frames that never arrived and what the wire costs in ms. The line is drawn
along the very straight line the model is computed on, so the moment the bar drops as the
line touches a rack is the same fact as "the LIDAR reports that rectangle" -- the radio
counts crossings with the LIDAR's own ray test (`sensors._ray_rect`), which is why the two
cannot disagree about which walls exist.
The model (`mecanum_lab/wifi.py`, stdlib math, no WiFi stack and no wish to have one):
rssi = tx_dbm - 10 n log10(d / d0) - (walls crossed) wall_db + shadow     [dBm]
q    = clamp((rssi - floor_dbm) / (good_dbm - floor_dbm), 0, 1)
Three numbers to check with a tape measure and the readout line, in `production` with the
AP below and the fade at zero: free floor 2 m from the AP gives -47.2 dBm and q 1.00. The
middle of the south aisle, 9 m and nothing in between, gives -62.9 dBm, q 0.63, 14 % of the
frames lost and 35 ms instead of 20. The far side of two racks at 15 m gives -92.2 dBm,
q 0.00 and no link at all. Every one of those is the formula above with the numbers from
this file in it; drive them and see.
The exercise, four steps and ten minutes:
1. Drive the first command above and hold `Up` in the south aisle. Nothing stands between
you and the AP, so q falls with distance alone: 1.00 at the spawn, 0.63 at x = 10 m,
0.43 at the far end at 18 m. Read the bar on the way: at q 0.43 one frame in three
never arrives and every one that does is 43 ms late instead of 20 ms. The robot still
drives -- that is the lesson of the first half, a bad link is not a stopped robot.
2. Turn north in the east aisle at x = 19 m. Between y = 3.69 and y = 4.58 m the line to
the AP starts crossing the racks at (13.5, 3.5)-(17, 5.5) and (13.5, 8)-(17, 10), and
q falls from 0.42 to 0.08 to 0.00 in two steps of `wall_db` each. One rack, not two,
is already below the level a robot can be driven on. Walls, not metres, kill a link.
3. Stand there and wait 1.5 s. The log says `link to 'muster' down at -82.1 dBm`, the
robot's outline turns amber, `/sim/robots` says `mode: autonomy`, and from that moment
nothing you type arrives at all -- the teleop keys keep publishing and the counters keep
climbing, and the robot does not move. `wifi.link_timeout` is how long the low level
has to last before that happens, and `wifi.link_up_q` (0.15) is the level it counts
against.
4. The same drive with the other onboard rule: `--set wifi.autonomy=dead_reckoning`. Now
the robot keeps executing the last command that really arrived, so it drives on at
whatever speed it was told to -- into the shelf in front of it. That is what "the robot
walks itself home" means on a real machine, and it is a decision about the practice car
and not about the radio: which of the two rules a robot in your hall should ship is a
question for the practice team.
The AP belongs to the hall: `wifi.ap_by_world.production = [1.0, 2.0]`, above the loading
area at the west wall next to the door the robots start at. That is where the one AP of a
hall this size goes in reality -- a technician mounts it where the cable run and a power
outlet are, which is a wall and not the middle of the ceiling above the racks -- and it is
why the shadow of the room sits in the north-east quarter. Move it and the shadow moves
with it: `--set wifi.ap=[10,6]` hangs it over the middle of the floor and the rack rows stop
mattering. Which of the layers won is on `/sim/config` under `wifi.effective_ap`, so neither
you nor a student has to guess.
Two knobs to play with after that, both of them numbers and not mysteries: `wifi.tx_dbm` is
the level at one metre (-40 dBm is a normal AP; a robot whose antenna sits behind a steel
chassis is nearer -45 dBm, and at -45 dBm about a third of this hall's free floor is then
below the failsafe level). `wifi.wall_db` is what one crossing costs: 12 dB is the middle of
what is measured at 2.4 GHz through loaded shelving, a wooden table alone is 3-6 dB, a steel
rack full of tools is 15-20 dB. `--set wifi.wall_db=6` and drive the east aisle again: the
steps halve and the far corner stays drivable -- one number, one whole corner of the hall.
What this model does NOT do (the limits are in the module's docstring, and saying them is
part of the exercise): one AP with one omnidirectional antenna, no second AP and no roaming,
no shared airtime, no multipath -- attenuation only, `gps.zones` is where multi-path lives --
and no retransmission, so a bad link here is lossy and slow but never out of order and never
duplicated. A real 802.11 station fixes a lost frame by sending it again and that costs
time; here a lost frame is gone, which is why `p_drop` is allowed to be the whole story.
_comment_tail: The link is a sensor like the others: it measures the radio, not the floor.
